plan.focus: The gap between Jack London's business growth and the displacement pressure on the workers who power it — told through Tre Mingo and the people on the ledger at the Port, Green & Gold, and Anchor Build.

sources.name: Tre Mingo
sources.quote: I walk past that fence every day. The development's not for me — it's happening around me. I work at the port, I've got three kids, and I'm watching rents climb while the people I work with talk about leaving. The businesses are growing, the numbers look good, but the folks on the ledger aren't the ones who get to stay. I don't feel like I'm part of it. I feel like I'm watching it from the other side of the fence.

sources.name: Marguerite Salcedo
sources.quote: Look, I run the numbers every day. Anchor Build is growing — 13.7%, 181 people on the payroll. That's real. But I'd be lying if I said I don't see the squeeze. My crews — the electricians, the laborers, the folks swinging hammers — they're the ones building these new units, and half of them can't afford to live in the buildings they're putting up. That's not a talking point, that's what I hear at the job site. I've got guys driving in from Antioch, from Stockton, because Jack London rent went up again. We're not pricing out strangers — we're pricing out the people who pour the concrete. And that keeps me up at night, because I've been in this business long enough to know you can't build a neighborhood on the backs of people who can't stay in it.

sources.name: Elle Lilo
sources.quote: I've been on that water for thirty-nine years, and I've watched this neighborhood grow up around the port. The numbers going up—the cranes, the new buildings—that's real. But I'll tell you what I see from the wheelhouse: the same faces showing up at the union hall, the same guys on the dock at 5 a.m. Tre Mingo's one of them. The work's steady, but the cost of living here keeps climbing, and I watch good people do the math on whether they can stay. I moved myself, just a few miles, to make it work. That's the part nobody puts on a spreadsheet—the quiet decisions people make every day to keep doing the job they love in the place they grew up.

excludedLeads.text: I could point you to a couple of my foremen who've told me they're looking at moving their families out of Oakland entirely — but I don't have names I can give you.
